description.narrative:
The Catholic Church in Nigeria has a long standing tradition of working for justice and integral human development, and providing care for marginalized members of society. This function is typically fulfilled through a network of established structures such as schools, health facilities, parish health committees, and lay organizations. These structures are in turn coordinated at the level of the diocese by Diocesan Education, Health, and Justice Development and Peace Commissions in each of the 54 Catholic dioceses which cover the entire country. Through these structures, the Church is able to address a broad range of development issues.
Catholic Caritas Foundation of Nigeria (CCFN) was established by the Catholic Bishops Conference of Nigeria (CBCN) in 2010 as a specialized development agency responsible for capacity building and coordination of development programs for the Catholic Church. Since the establishment of CCFN, the agency has been engaged in various interventions in the areas of Emergency and Humanitarian Response, Health and HIV/AIDS, Governance, Food Security, Agriculture, and Livelihoods. CCFN does not implement projects directly, but through the Provincial and Diocesan Structures described above. At the current time, over 95% of CCFN’s funding comes from international donors. These donor funds are typically tied to specific program activities and must be applied in geographical locations which reflect the priorities of the donors. CCFN often receives requests from diocesan partners to collaborate with them on tailored development projects that will address key needs in specific communities, but is unable to respond to such requests due to non-availability of funds. CCFN is also financially handicapped in the area of responding to emergencies, a key area of CCFNs mandate as the national Caritas organization.
An additional role of CCFN is that of supporting and strengthening the capacity of the provincial and diocesan partners to carry out their humanitarian and development work effectively and efficiently. CCFN therefore needs to retain a core complement of skilled staff to accompany the partners. Although capacity-strengthening work ultimately impacts on the quality of services delivered by partners to beneficiaries, it does not directly target service beneficiaries. Funding for capacity-building can therefore be challenging to secure, as the outcomes and impacts are often long-term and sometimes intangible, and can be difficult to measure objectively.
